extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and critics of architecture; educated general public interested in architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A Victorian-era critical framework for judging and producing architecture by identifying its essential virtues (action, speech, and appearance) and practical divisions (construction, decoration, walls/roofs/apertures). Intended to teach lay and specialist readers how to form rapid, rational judgments about buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three great branches of architectural virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "We have thus, altogether, three great branches of architectural virtue, and we require of any building,— 1. That it act well... 2. That it speak well... 3. That it look well."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting = do the practical duty (defend from weather/violence). Speaking = the duty of monuments/churches to record and express. Looking = pleasing presence regardless of other duties. Use these three as first-order dimensions when judging a building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act well: performance of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "That it act well, and do the things it was intended to do in the best way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A building must fulfill its intended function effectively. Evaluation includes whether it defends, shelters, carries, or holds in the simplest and most appropriate manner (see examples: lighthouse must stand firm and carry a light). Consider forces to be resisted and efficiency of means; avoid over-expenditure of materials or complexity unnecessary for the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak well: clarity and force of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: "That it speak well, and say the things it was intended to say in the best words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concerns a building's communicative role (monuments, churches as 'books of history'). The author cautions that general laws cannot reliably govern expression because of conventions and differing audiences; to judge expression you must place yourself in the original sympathetic position of the intended spectators and understand the symbols and associations used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look well: beauty as pleasing presence
rubrics_metrics.description: "That it look well, and please us by its presence, whatever it has to do or say."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearance/beauty is a distinct virtue. The writer treats it as a canon of loveliness that can be discerned and applied so a passerby may distinguish noble from ignoble work quickly. Beauty is partly judged by the imagination and intentions of the builder as revealed in the decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable virtues: Strength and Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The two qualities of buildings which can be justly weighed are their strength (good construction) and their beauty (good decoration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strength is judged by simplicity, efficiency, knowledge of forces, and appropriate arrangements of materials. Beauty is judged by the quality of decoration and whether it expresses genuine affections and delight in higher works (nature/God's work). Both testify to the intelligence or imagination of the builder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction must be simple and economical
rubrics_metrics.description: A building is well built if it answers its purpose in the simplest way, "with no over-expenditure of means."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the design uses just the materials and arrangements necessary to resist expected forces and serve its function; e.g., a lighthouse that uses excessive stone is not well built even if it endures. Understanding of technical constraints and optimal arrangements is required to judge well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admire the builder's intellect, not mere manual skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should admire the choice, invention, and application of means (choice of curve, numbering of stones, knowledge of tides/soil/forces) rather than the visible technical dexterity of masons or carpenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment focuses on mental power: the planning, foresight, and engineering judgement expressed in the work. Technical dexterity is not unimportant, but the evaluative emphasis is on intellectual contribution and resolution in overcoming difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration must indicate honest, strong liking
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first thing we have to ask of the decoration is that it should indicate strong liking, and that honestly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament should show that the builder genuinely enjoys and loves the ornamented subject (example: Bourges Cathedral's hawthorn). Anti-patterns include pretending to like stylistic motifs (e.g., triglyphs) purely for fashion or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration must like the right things (delight in God's work)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The right thing to be liked is God's work... And all noble ornamentation is the expression of man's delight in God's work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prescribes that ornamentation ideally expresses delight in nature/creation (interpreted as 'God's work'). Decorations fixed on wholesome, natural, or divinely-ordered subjects are preferable to those celebrating base or trivial tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hypocrisy in taste; prefer genuine instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Many faults of architecture arise not from honest mistaken choice but from hypocrisy—professing to like things one does not truly enjoy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics/architects should cultivate and consult their natural instincts and tastes. Teaching people to feel and to speak plainly about what they like precedes correcting mistaken liking. False adoption of stylistic affectations should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression cannot be fully legalized; consider original audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression (the 'speaking' virtue) cannot be made into a general law because of conventional alphabets and the need to be in the sympathetic position of original viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging expressive or symbolic aspects, attempt to understand the original conventions and the intended audience's associations; otherwise do not insist on universal criteria for expressive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layable laws for construction and canons of loveliness
rubrics_metrics.description: There are universal laws with respect to a building's performance of its necessary work and 'divine canons of loveliness' that admit no ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are intended to allow rapid practical judgement about common buildings; understanding basic structural laws enables immediate recognition of noble vs. ignoble work and dismissal of styles at variance with these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate usefulness and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament and construction have no necessary connection and should not be reasoned from one to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasures of ornament are independent from the satisfactions of construction. Attempts to rationalize beauty by utility (or vice versa) will blunt the sense of beauty or degrade the appreciation of construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach people first to feel, then to judge
rubrics_metrics.description: Logically one might invert the order, but practically the author insists: first teach people to speak plainly about what they like; then teach which likings are right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional approach: encourage spontaneous, honest aesthetic responses first; after that, provide corrective principles to refine taste. Many modern architects build from received rules rather than genuine liking—this must be countered by cultivating honest taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional classification: Architecture of Protection vs Position
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical duties of buildings are twofold: (1) to hold and protect something (architecture of protection); (2) to place or carry something (architecture of position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this functional division to determine requirements: protective architecture concerns walls, roofs, and apertures (including comfort of habitation); positional architecture concerns bridges, aqueducts, staircases, towers, lighthouses, chimneys, etc. Each functional class has different evaluation priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective architecture's three members: walls, roofs, apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective architecture has to wall a space, to roof it, and to give access to it, of persons, light, and air; thus consider walls, roofs, and apertures as its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging buildings whose purpose is protection/habitation, analyze how well each of these three elements performs. Floor/paving are secondary unless the flooring is also a roof; the architect's main domain is walls, roofs, apertures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common buildings admit rapid, rational judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Of common buildings, built in common circumstances, every man, woman, or child can form judgment both rational and rapid; their necessary or possible features are few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the simple laws of structure; after a few hours' study one can detect whether ordinary buildings obey structural laws and thereby discard many styles as unnatural or monstrous.
